subject: physics
question_text: Why can a heat engine with 100% efficiency never be realised in practice?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Very Short Answer Question 21 (printed p.126). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: for an ideal (Carnot) engine η = 1 − T₂/T₁, so η = 1 requires a sink at absolute zero, which cannot be reached; this is the same limit the Kelvin-Planck statement expresses directly, that no engine working in a cycle converts heat from a single reservoir entirely into work.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.margin_note: First mark. Write η = 1 − T₂/T₁ for an ideal engine between source T₁ and sink T₂.
steps.why: This is the limit on efficiency set by the second law, so a claim of 100% efficiency can be checked directly against it.
common_mistakes: Writing η = 1 − T₁/T₂ with the temperatures swapped. T₂, the sink, always goes on top.
Forgetting the temperatures must be on the absolute (kelvin) scale, not Celsius.

recall.must_convey: That an ideal engine's efficiency is one minus T two by T one, with T one the source and T two the sink, both on the absolute scale.
accept: eta equals one minus T two by T one
source temperature T one, sink T two
reject: Q one is R T one log V two by V one
heard_as: eta equals one minus T two by T one

steps.memory_tip: The sink temperature T₂ is always the one on top of the fraction that gets subtracted.

steps.label: Why 100% cannot be reached
lines: η = 1 needs T₂ = 0, a sink at absolute
zero, which no real process can reach.
The Kelvin-Planck statement says the same
thing directly: no engine can convert heat
from one reservoir completely into work.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Say η = 1 needs a sink at absolute zero, which the second law rules out.
steps.why: The formula and the Kelvin-Planck statement express the same limit in two different ways, one by calculation and one by direct statement.
common_mistakes: Saying 100% efficiency is impossible only because of friction or other real-world losses. Even an ideal, loss-free engine stays below 100% efficiency.
Leaving the reason at "the second law forbids it" without saying what that means for T₂ or the reservoir.

recall.must_convey: That η = 1 would need a sink at absolute zero, which cannot be reached, and that this is the same limit the Kelvin-Planck statement expresses directly.
accept: needs a sink at absolute zero
reject: heat cannot flow from a colder body to a hotter one

steps.memory_tip: 100% efficiency needs a sink at absolute zero — and absolute zero is never reached.

insider_note: Give both the formula reason (T₂ = 0 is unreachable) and the Kelvin-Planck reason — the two together are the complete answer to this question.
